reference.source: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
clinicalPearls: Presents with intermittent dysphagia to both solids and liquids and non-cardiac chest pain that can mimic angina
Symptoms are episodic and may be provoked by stress, hot or cold liquids, or reflux
High-resolution manometry defines the disorder by premature (spastic) distal contractions with a shortened distal latency and preserved oesophagogastric junction relaxation
Barium swallow may show a corkscrew or rosary-bead appearance during a spastic episode, but is often normal between attacks
Cardiac causes of chest pain must be excluded before attributing symptoms to the oesophagus
Treatment targets the spasm and pain with smooth-muscle relaxants and neuromodulators, with peroral endoscopic myotomy reserved for refractory disease
Coexisting gastro-oesophageal reflux can trigger or worsen spastic contractions and should be sought and treated
reference.pathophysiology: Distal oesophageal spasm is a motility disorder characterised by uncoordinated, simultaneous or premature contractions of the distal oesophageal smooth muscle. Impaired inhibitory neuronal signalling, particularly a deficiency of nitric-oxide-mediated inhibition, shortens the normal latency between swallowing and contraction, so that contractions occur prematurely and out of sequence. This disordered propagation disrupts orderly bolus transit, producing intermittent dysphagia, while the vigorous, poorly coordinated contractions generate episodic chest pain.
additionalDifferentials: Functional chest pain of oesophageal origin
additionalInvestigations: High-resolution oesophageal manometry to characterise contraction latency and vigour
Barium oesophagram to look for corkscrew/rosary-bead morphology
Upper endoscopy to exclude mucosal disease, eosinophilic oesophagitis, and obstruction
Cardiac evaluation to exclude ischaemic chest pain
Ambulatory reflux monitoring where reflux may be a trigger
redFlags: Chest pain with features suggesting cardiac ischaemia
Progressive dysphagia, weight loss, or regurgitation suggesting achalasia or malignancy
Odynophagia or alarm features warranting mucosal assessment
reference.prognosis: The course is variable and often benign, with many patients managed symptomatically; a minority have refractory pain or dysphagia, and some overlap with or progress towards spastic achalasia.
pitfalls: Attributing chest pain to the oesophagus before excluding cardiac disease
Diagnosing spasm on a single abnormal swallow rather than a consistent manometric pattern
Missing spastic achalasia, which is managed differently
Overlooking reflux as a treatable trigger of spastic contractions
references: Sleisenger and Fordtran's Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
Chicago Classification of oesophageal motility disorders
